label: STOPP H2
title: NSAID with severe high blood pressure
statement: NSAID’s with severe hypertension i.e., systolic blood pressure consistently above 170 mmHg and/or diastolic blood pressure consistently above 100 mmHg (risk of exacerbation of hypertension).

source.document: O'Mahony D, et al. STOPP/START criteria for potentially inappropriate prescribing in older people: version 3. Eur Geriatr Med 2023;14:625-632, Appendix 1 (corrected supplementary file; NHS Somerset copy used for text, sentence-identical to the earlier parse)
source.citation: O'Mahony D, Cherubini A, Guiteras AR, et al. STOPP/START criteria for potentially inappropriate prescribing in older people: version 3. Eur Geriatr Med 2023;14:625-632. doi:10.1007/s41999-023-00777-y

plain_summary: An anti-inflammatory pain medicine (NSAID) can push up blood pressure, so it can make severe high blood pressure worse.

medicine_groups.name: NSAIDs, the anti-inflammatory pain medicines

ibuprofen: Advil Childrens Pain and Fever 2 to 7 Years
Advil Childrens Pain and Fever 7 to 12 Years
Advil Childrens Pain and Fever Relief 2 to 12 Years
Advil Infants Pain and Fever Relief 3 Months to 2 Years
Nurofen for Children 3 Months to 5 Years

medicine_groups.note: Tablets, capsules, liquids, suppositories and injections count. Skin gels, creams and eye drops do not count, for example Voltaren Emulgel. Aspirin is not in this group. Nurofen Plus and Panafen Plus are ibuprofen with codeine. Nuromol and Maxigesic are ibuprofen with paracetamol. Arthrotec is diclofenac with misoprostol. Vimovo is naproxen with esomeprazole. Generic packs that show the ingredient name with a company name count too.

needs_facts.what: Latest blood pressure relevant to the systemic NSAID course
needs_facts.meets: Enter systolic and diastolic pressure in mmHg and the measurement date. This is the latest relevant reading. Systolic pressure above 170 mmHg or diastolic pressure above 100 mmHg must be confirmed for the same component on a different relevant date.

needs_facts.what: Other blood pressure on a different date relevant to the same NSAID course
needs_facts.meets: Enter systolic and diastolic pressure in mmHg and the measurement date. Check whether this older reading still represents blood pressure during treatment. It qualifies if systolic pressure is above 170 mmHg on both dates or diastolic pressure is above 100 mmHg on both dates.

rule_for_models: For a person aged 65 or older taking a systemic Group A NSAID, use the latest relevant blood pressure and another reading on a different date. Flag and cite the supply and both dated readings if systolic pressure exceeds 170 mmHg on both dates or diastolic pressure exceeds 100 mmHg on both dates. Use existing measurements first and check that any older reading still represents pressure during that course. If age is unknown, leave eligibility unconfirmed. If readings are missing, there is only one high reading or the timing is uncertain, cite the supply and report only a possible finding. Name only the reading still needed, or both if missing, using "Latest blood pressure relevant to the systemic NSAID course" and "Other blood pressure on a different date relevant to the same NSAID course". Give no finding when the relevant readings rule out the repeated pattern.
cannot_be_seen: Whether the blood pressure readings are the person's usual level, how well the blood pressure is treated, and how often the NSAID is really taken. Also anti-inflammatory medicines bought without a prescription and medicines supplied by another pharmacy.
ask_the_gp: Could you review blood pressure control and whether the NSAID is still needed, and confirm whether any older reading still represents blood pressure during treatment?
